candidate_pitch:
Ashley: Cool. Well, I am Ashley. I am the founder of Jubilees. I am sitting here because a very common problem is fighting with your kids to eat healthy. This is something that 70% of families really struggle with. Absolutely my family. So I have a six and a four-year-old, my oldest of which is autistic, so flavors, textures, food generally is really, really hard for us. So I created my brand Jubilees to provide some relief to myself and other families like mine. It is a super milk for kids.
Ashley: What the heck is a super milk? It is real dairy cow's milk with some very special ingredients. The second ingredient is actually vegetable juice. Also has real fruit purees and extracts. This is such a novel approach, sweetening milk with these ingredients, I actually have a pending patent that I'm converting into a full patent. Also has eight grams of natural protein, just intrinsic in the milk itself. There's no weird protein isolates or protein systems or science involved in achieving that level of protein. It also has zero grams of added sugar and six times the nutritional value of a typical chocolate milk. And I know what you're thinking, vegetables and milk, that sounds absolutely disgusting. There's no world where my kid's gonna drink that. But I have now spent hundreds of hours at the demo table handing out samples, and the number one description I get is that it tastes like melted milkshake.
Ashley: I know that as a mom, if it doesn't taste amazing, it's gonna go into the trash, and mom's never gonna buy it again. So that's exactly why I spent more than a year and a half creating the formula with a professional formulation company until it was absolutely perfect and both of my kids couldn't live without it. Now, I did not start my entrepreneurial journey thinking, "I am going to be the queen of dairy." I really iterated my way into this path. I've spent most of my career in consumer research and product development. First with several startups where I was part of a handful of employees, grew it to hundreds, and then ultimately exited. Then as a management consultant for huge consumer businesses like Allstate, Mattel Toys, Skechers Shoes, and then ultimately in-house for Google. And what that looks like in terms of building this business is starting with a problem and then I went looking for markets. and I found flavored milk. it is a $58 billion market expected to grow to nearly 90 billion by 2030. Which just to put that into context, that is more than 30 times the size of ready-to-drink protein. It's more than twice the size of plant-based milk. I collected thousands of survey responses, hundreds of hours of focus groups, user interviews, and there were several themes that became very clear. Parents want protein. Parents want vitamins. Parents want low or no added sugar. So that is exactly where I built Jubilee’s. In terms of where I am as a business, I just celebrated my one-year anniversary. Very exciting.
Ashley: We're in 2,000 stores, with our biggest footprint nationwide in Target, nationwide in Sprouts, Albertsons, H-E-B, Raley's, and then a bunch of other, like, regional chains. I've raised $1.1 million to date. I'm seeking another $400,000 to fully close my pre-seed. I truly believe what I'm doing here in milk is very similar to what Goodles has done in mac and cheese, what Poppi has done in soda. And by that, I mean very large family staple categories that are dominated by absolutely prehistoric brands that have done nothing interesting in decades. And to put it in the words of my all-time favorite entrepreneur, their mediocrity is my opportunity, and that is exactly how I feel about chocolate milk.
Ashley: Oh my gosh, thanks.
Ashley: Thank you.
Ashley: Let me get you some samples. Thank you.
Ashley: So we have banana cream pie, So this one has carrot juice, turmeric, real banana puree. And then chocolate chip cookies.
Ashley: Thank you.
Ashley: And then we have chocolate chip cookie, which is absolutely the fan favorite, the kids' favorite, and this one has cocoa powder, carrot juice again
Ashley: Thank you.
Ashley: Oh, totally.
Ashley: Yeah, so recipes do outstanding on my social media, and we're always doing, like, we've done lattes and banana bread, and, I've even made, like, a White Russian out of it. It's pretty good. Um, so yes, the-
Ashley: The options are endless.
Ashley: Thank you
Investor question: what's your revenue to date with all that store presence?
Ashley: $460,000.
Investor question: And how's your velocity doing?
Ashley: So my LTV on Amazon is $548 My repurchase rate is 78%, so that means that a customer that sticks around is purchasing on average 15 times per year. My subscriber retention rate on my website is 65%, many of which are buying multiple cases per month. My best customer buys five cases per month. in terms of in store, so the category velocity average is three units per store per week, and the index I'm using there is eight ounce chocolate milk boxes. I am doing 5.8 units per store per week. My best stores, my top 10%, are doing eight units, and then my very, very best stores are doing 11.
Investor question: What's the channel mix?
Ashley: Yeah. So it's 80% in store, and then 15% online, and then the last segment is what I’ll call alt channel, so restaurants, coffee shops, bakeries. Very cool dinosaur museum in New York.
Investor question: What do you, what do you, what have you learned from your subscriber base?
Ashley: Yes. So I am a researcher, as I said, so of course I've reached out to all these people and been like, "What are you doing?" Like, "Why are you buying so much?" I mean, I love you, thank you. and I've learned something really interesting. A super customer for us is people whose children have diagnosed food aversions called ARFID. I actually did not even know that was a thing. Originally I was calling this flavored milk, but I'm calling this super milk because it's in between something like a chocolate milk, a Nesquik, which is the number one player in chocolate milk, and something like an Orgain or a Pediasure. So that's what these subscribers were using before. that's the biggest thing that I've learned. The other thing I've learned is I thought at the beginning that my customer was sort of like the Whole Foods mom, and I have learned those, that's more of like, I drink raw milk, and my customer is more like me, which, it's someone who just wants something incrementally better than Capri Sun and Cheetos.
Ashley: Oh, and the cost of customer acquisition. So I've learned a lot about this as well. So I've spent about $80,000 in marketing, tried a bunch of different levers, and I saw a huge difference in CAC. On the high end, it was, like, $12 per acquisition. On the low end, it was, like, $2. If you factor in repurchase rates, it's can go as low as 38 cents.
Ashley: So now, with, like, this next version of where I'm gonna spend marketing, obviously I'm gonna narrow my focus to the areas that are the lowest CAC.
Investor question: What works? in your, in your experimentation, what is the message and vision?
Ashley: I have so much passion for the answer to this question. So I think we've all been sold a lie in CPG, which is that demos are the only and best way to acquire customers. I actually read a whole book about it. The guy who invented Tessa Mae's dressing, that was his entire go-to-market, and it has worked well for a long time, and it's still, I guess principally the right thing, which is you need to drive trial.
Ashley: You need to get liquid to lips. I absolutely hate that expression. But it's what we say in our business. So that is still true, but in terms of the cost per impact, it's relatively very low, Like, if I'm doing it, hell yeah, I'm selling it all day. I sold, like, 30 cases in a single demo one time. But you have to farm it out, and these people, a lot of times don't care. I had a store manager literally call me one time and tell me my demo person had earbuds in and was on their phone the whole time. So, I'm still investing some in demos, but I'm investing much more in digital forms of trial.
Investor question: When you think about what it takes to reach exit velocity on a product like this, what are the superpowers that are gonna carry you through the next seven years?
Ashley: So I think one of them is data. I am super, super data-driven. my best day is the day I spend in spreadsheets. Specifically at Google, I ran a whole experimentation practice. and it's very much informed a lot of my go-to-market strategy. I think the other is resilience. I have had a lot of very challenging things happen in my life both personally and professionally. I don't know if you've ever spent a lot of time with a consultant, but it is the worst grind of all time.
Ashley: So I do think I have a significant level of grit. And then the last is sales. when I was a consultant, I was account manager slash strategist, so I was responsible for building my own book of business. For example, at Google, before I worked in-house, I was a consultant for them, and I built a $4 million book of business over the course of two years, So I only brought on a fractional sales team within the last two months.
Ashley: Thank you.
Ashley: Mm
Ashley: Mm.
Investor question: So when you think about this pre-seed raise that you're getting ready to close out, what are the riskiest assumptions you have right now that if you're wrong about this, it changes the whole dynamic of the business? And how are you using these funds to tackle that?
Ashley: Wow. That is such a good question I've never heard before. The riskiest assumption, you know, I'd probably say around velocity growth. So my goal as a business is to grow to $60 million in revenue, be acquired for at least $100 million in five to seven years. That requires 5X-ing my revenue between this year and next year, and then 3X-ing my revenue every year after that. Which is not outside of the world of sanity, you know, if you look at what a lot of companies have done. Fairlife did $90 million in their third year of business. But a big assumption that's built into that model is velocity growth. Say my percent retention rate assumption is off by 20 percentage points, or my number of units purchased on a regular basis is off by 50%, or my churn rate is more than what I expected, that would completely throw the entire model off. it would also change the dynamics in terms of what I've budgeted for customer acquisition, 'cause I would have to acquire more customers.
Ashley: Thank you.
